source_refs.note: Topic 16.7 with Examples 16.7-16.8 (PDF 74-76); the V-Q graph (printed 'Fig 16.15', text Fig 16.10) is redrawn. Example 16.7 is solved with its stated 100 V; the book's 120 V working is reported in a warning. The check question is MCQ 8.

blocks.text: A capacitor can be thought of as a device for storing electrical energy as well as charge. The charge on the plates has electrical potential energy, because work must be done to place charge on the plates. Good evidence comes from discharging: if the plates of a charged capacitor are joined by a thick wire, charge flows from one plate to the other and the wire becomes hot. The heat must have come from energy stored in the charged capacitor.

Since Q is proportional to V, a graph of V against Q is a straight line through the origin (Fig 16.10). Each small increment of charge raises the potential difference, so a larger amount of work is needed to bring up the next increment. Divide the area under the graph into thin strips of width dQ. The work to move a small charge dQ through a potential difference V1 is dW = (dQ)(V1) (16.38), equal to the area of one strip. The total work to charge the capacitor to Q is the sum of all such strips, the area of triangle OAB: (1/2)(OA)(AB) = (1/2) QV. So the energy stored in a charged capacitor is W = (1/2) QV (16.39), and with Q = CV, W = (1/2) CV^2 (16.40).

blocks.alt: A graph of V against Q: a straight pink line from the origin O to B, above the point A on the Q axis. Under the line are ten narrow rectangles of width delta Q forming a staircase; one rectangle, at the level V1, is hatched. Dotted lines mark V1 and the final potential V on the V axis.

blocks.text: The energy can also be regarded as stored in the electric field between the plates. Substituting V = Ed and C = A eo er / d gives energy = (1/2)(A eo er / d)(Ed)^2 = (1/2) eo er E^2 (Ad) (16.42), where Ad is the volume between the plates. This relation is valid for any electric field strength.

Capacitors of 4 uF and 8 uF are connected in series and charged by a 100 V supply. Find the total charge and the energy stored. Solution: 1/Ce = 1/4 + 1/8 = 3/8, so Ce = (8/3) uF. Q = Ce V = (8/3 x 10^-6 F)(100 V) = 2.67 x 10^-4 C. W = (1/2) QV = (1/2)(2.67 x 10^-4 C)(100 V) = 1.33 x 10^-2 J.

A 16 uF capacitor is charged to 100 V. Find the energy stored. If the potential difference is doubled, by what factor does the energy increase? Solution: W = (1/2) CV^2 = (1/2)(16 x 10^-6 F)(100 V)^2 = 8 x 10^-2 J. The energy depends on V^2, so if V is doubled the energy increases by a factor of 2^2 = 4.
